title: Timers
lede: WHATWG/browser-standard timer functions as bare globals, matching real JS rather than a namespace. The one recurring divergence is that a timer callback must be a zero-argument, void-returning closure value — a bare reference to a top-level named function isn't accepted yet. Under the hood there's no phased event loop: setTimeout, setInterval, and setImmediate share a single flat fire-time-ordered queue that drains after the synchronous script, while queueMicrotask has its own FIFO drained before that queue.

entries.name: setTimeout(fn, ms) / clearTimeout(id)
entries.signature: setTimeout(fn: () => void, ms: number): number; clearTimeout(id: number): void
entries.description: Schedules a callback to fire once after ms milliseconds and returns an id; clearTimeout cancels it before it fires. These are bare global functions, matching real JS (not a namespace). Multiple timeouts fire in delay order, not registration order.
differences: Callback is restricted to a zero-argument, `void`-returning function — an arrow/function-expression closure, or a bare reference to a top-level named function.

entries.name: setInterval(fn, ms) / clearInterval(id)
entries.signature: setInterval(fn: () => void, ms: number): number; clearInterval(id: number): void
entries.description: Schedules a callback to repeat every ms milliseconds until cleared. Closures capture by reference, so the idiomatic self-cancelling pattern — a callback that reads the id its own declaration produces — works correctly. Same callback scope as setTimeout.

entries.name: setImmediate(fn) / clearImmediate(id)
entries.signature: setImmediate(fn: () => void): number; clearImmediate(id: number): void
entries.description: Schedules a callback to run as soon as possible, reusing the exact same timer queue as a delay-0 setTimeout — clearImmediate is clearTimeout under another name. Fires after the synchronous script alongside the rest of the timer queue.
differences: Real Node guarantees `setImmediate` fires before a same-tick `setTimeout(fn, 0)` when scheduled from inside an I/O callback, because its event loop has distinct phases (check vs. timers); this compiler's timer drain is a single flat fire-time-ordered queue with no phase concept, so the two are genuinely indistinguishable here (both fire at "now").

entries.name: queueMicrotask(fn)
entries.description: Queues a callback onto a real microtask FIFO, distinct from the timer queue, drained after the synchronous script and before any timers fire.
